rationale: The exact entry's core is carried directly by Zechariah 6:5 (four spirits/ruach that stand before the Lord and go forth) together with the matching colored-horse imagery of Zechariah 6 and Revelation 6:1-8; the fourfold outgoing pattern is likewise explicit in Genesis 2:10 (and echoed in Revelation 22:1). These texts identify personal, throne-dispatched agents rather than bare compass points. The common directional-idiom reading is acknowledged as the surface sense of several passages, yet it must still treat Zechariah 6:5 as an exception or secondary overlay; the entry's agent reading absorbs the directional reach (four quarters) without contradiction and unifies the horse, spirit, and river texts under one referent. No supplied detail is left unexplained by the core, so the entry is the stronger account.
book_core_identification: The four winds are the four spirits of heaven—God's executing agents—shown as the four horsemen.
book_secondary_elaborations: The same fourfold outgoing pattern appears in the river dividing from Eden.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In mainstream usage 'the four winds' is simply the ancient idiom for the four cardinal directions, hence a merism for worldwide extent or 'everywhere'; any personal or angelic overtones are secondary and context-bound.
counter_core_identification: Four winds = four cardinal directions / universal geographic scope.
material_core_denial: The four winds are not personal spirit-agents dispatched from the throne but an impersonal directional idiom.
counter_case: Matthew 24:31 / Mark 13:27 gather the elect 'from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other,' language that most naturally denotes spatial extremities.
Daniel 8:8; 11:4 and Zechariah 2:6 use 'four winds of heaven' for territorial division or scattering in every direction.
Jeremiah 49:36 and Revelation 7:1 locate the winds at the four quarters/corners, reinforcing the compass-point reading.
Standard lexicons and commentaries treat the phrase as a fixed merism for totality, with ruach's spirit sense appearing only locally.
book_explanatory_advantages: Zechariah 6:5 explicitly names the four horse-drawn chariots 'the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord,' supplying the agent identity in so many words.
The identical colored-horse motif links Zechariah's spirits directly to Revelation 6:1-8's four horsemen, giving a single referent across both visions.

Genesis 2:10's river that 'went out' from the divine presence and parted into four heads supplies an independent fourfold-outgoing pattern from the same throne source, matching the spirits' departure.
The agent reading still accounts for universal reach (they cover the four quarters) while also explaining why the winds can be held, sent, or recalled—actions impossible for bare directions.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The directional gloss is immediately intelligible in every 'from/to the four winds' gathering or scattering text without further symbolic machinery.
It aligns with ordinary ancient Near-Eastern usage of 'four winds' as a geographic merism.
